summary.text: Assuming the first claimed identity makes the shifted terms satisfy a Fibonacci recurrence; using the finitely computed values at indices 3773 and 3774, a fast-doubling Fibonacci calculation modulo \(195318521017\) shows that this number divides both \(a_{249580077006}\) and \(a_{249580077007}\). Thus their gcd \(g>1\); writing their sum as \(gt\) with \(t>1\), the true next term is \(g+t\), whereas the claimed value is \(1+gt\), impossible since \(1+gt-(g+t)=(g-1)(t-1)>0\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(a_1=a_2=1\), and for \(n\geq 3\) let
\[
a_n=g_n+\frac{a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}}{g_n},
\qquad g_n=\gcd(a_{n-1},a_{n-2}).
\]
We will show that it is impossible for the first asserted identity
\[
 a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}                                      \tag{1}
\]
to hold for every \(n\geq3775\). This already disproves the conjunction of the three identities in the conjecture; the other two identities need not be considered.

All terms \(a_n\) are positive. Indeed, this is true initially, and if the two preceding terms are positive, then their gcd is positive, so the defining expression for the next term is at least that positive gcd.

Assume, for a contradiction, that all three conjectured formulas hold for every \(n\geq3775\). In particular, (1) holds at every such index. Define
\[
 b_j=a_{j+3773}+1\qquad(j\geq0).
\]
Applying (1) at the index \(j+3775\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{j+2}
 &=a_{j+3775}+1\\
 &=2+a_{j+3774}+a_{j+3773}\\
 &=(a_{j+3774}+1)+(a_{j+3773}+1)\\
 &=b_{j+1}+b_j.
\end{aligned}                                                   \tag{2}
\]
Thus, under our assumption, the shifted sequence \(b_j\) obeys the Fibonacci recurrence from its first term onward.

Let the Fibonacci numbers be defined by \(F_0=0\), \(F_1=1\), and
\(F_{r+2}=F_{r+1}+F_r\). A standard induction using (2) gives
\[
 b_{j+1}=b_1F_{j+1}+b_0F_j.
\]
(The formula is immediate for \(j=0\); if it holds at two consecutive indices, both sides at the next index are the sums of their two preceding values.) Hence, for every \(j\geq0\),
\[
 a_{j+3774}+1
 =(a_{3774}+1)F_{j+1}+(a_{3773}+1)F_j.                         \tag{3}
\]
Notice that (3) has been derived solely from the supposition that (1) always holds. It is not being assumed as an additional conjectural formula.

We now use the modulus
\[
 p=195318521017
\]
and the index
\[
 k=249580073232.
\]
Direct finite evaluation of the original gcd recurrence from the initial values \(1,1\) through indices 3773 and 3774 gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{3774}={}&,\\[2mm]
a_{3773}={}&.
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{4}
\]
Here the finite evaluation means that, starting with \(a_1=a_2=1\), at each successive index one takes the gcd of the preceding two already obtained integers and applies the displayed defining recurrence. Thus (4) is an exact finite computation with the original sequence, independent of the conjecture.

Reducing the two coefficients needed in (3) modulo \(p\) gives
\[
 a_{3774}+1\equiv 99768150822\pmod p,
 \qquad
 a_{3773}+1\equiv 77940394259\pmod p.                          \tag{5}
\]

The required Fibonacci residues are
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_k&\equiv117378126758\pmod p,\\
F_{k+1}&\equiv21827756563\pmod p,\\
F_{k+2}&\equiv139205883321\pmod p.                             \tag{6}
\end{aligned}
\]
For completeness, these residues can be obtained without constructing the enormous Fibonacci numbers themselves. The binary expansion of \(k\) is
\[
 k=(11101000011100001000011011000100010000)_2.
\]
Starting from \((F_0,F_1)=(0,1)\), process these bits from left to right. If the pair for an index \(r\) is known, use the fast-doubling identities
\[
 F_{2r}=F_r(2F_{r+1}-F_r),
 \qquad
 F_{2r+1}=F_r^2+F_{r+1}^2,
\]
and
\[
 F_{2r+2}=F_{2r}+F_{2r+1}.
\]
For a processed bit 0 this gives the pair for \(2r\), and for a processed bit 1 it gives the pair for \(2r+1\). Reducing after each operation modulo \(p\), the final pair is
\[
(F_k,F_{k+1})\equiv(117378126758,21827756563)\pmod p.
\]
Adding these two residues gives the third residue in (6):
\[
117378126758+21827756563=139205883321<p.
\]
Thus (6) follows from a finite modular computation using only the Fibonacci recurrence identities.

We next apply the conditional closed form (3). First take \(j=k\). Since
\[
 k+3774=249580077006,
\]
equations (3), (5), and (6) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{249580077006}+1
&\equiv99768150822\cdot21827756563
   +77940394259\cdot117378126758\pmod p\\
&\equiv1\pmod p.                                                \tag{7}
\end{aligned}
\]
The final modular arithmetic can be checked explicitly: the unreduced weighted sum is
\[
11326212385784681827108
 =57988419771\,p+1.
\]
Subtracting 1 from (7) therefore shows
\[
 p\mid a_{249580077006}.                                        \tag{8}
\]

Next take \(j=k+1=249580073233\) in (3). Now
\[
 j+3774=249580077007,
\]
and therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{249580077007}+1
&\equiv99768150822\cdot139205883321
   +77940394259\cdot21827756563\pmod p\\
&\equiv1\pmod p.                                                \tag{9}
\end{aligned}
\]
Again, the arithmetic is displayed by the exact division
\[
15589577514788957011679
 =79816176334\,p+1.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 p\mid a_{249580077007}.                                        \tag{10}
\]

Set
\[
 m=249580077006,
 \qquad x=a_{m+1}=a_{249580077007},
 \qquad y=a_m=a_{249580077006},
\]
and let
\[
 g=\gcd(x,y).
\]
By (8) and (10), \(p\) is a common divisor of \(x\) and \(y\), so
\[
 p\mid g.
\]
The terms \(x,y\) are positive, hence \(g>0\). Since \(p>1\) and \(p\mid g\), it follows in particular that
\[
 g\geq2.                                                        \tag{11}
\]
Primality of \(p\) is not needed here; only \(p>1\) matters.

Because \(g\) divides both \(x\) and \(y\), it divides their sum. Write
\[
 x+y=gt
\]
with \(t\) a positive integer. In fact, positivity of \(x\) and \(y\), together with \(g\mid x\) and \(g\mid y\), implies \(x\geq g\) and \(y\geq g\). Therefore
\[
 x+y\geq2g,
\]
so
\[
 t\geq2.                                                        \tag{12}
\]

Consider now the next index
\[
 N=m+2=249580077008,

the announced horizon of the contradiction. The actual defining recurrence gives
\[
 a_N=g+\frac{x+y}{g}=g+t.                                       \tag{13}
\]
On the other hand, \(N\geq3775\), so our assumption that the conjecture holds everywhere requires its first formula at this same index:
\[
 a_N=1+x+y=1+gt.                                                \tag{14}
\]
But (11) and (12) make (13) and (14) incompatible, because
\[
 (1+gt)-(g+t)=gt-g-t+1=(g-1)(t-1)>0.
\]
Thus \(g+t\neq1+gt\), contradicting the two asserted values of \(a_N\).

We conclude that (1) cannot hold for every \(n\geq3775\). More precisely, if it held at all indices from 3775 through the derivation above, then the two consecutive terms at indices \(249580077006\) and \(249580077007\) would both be divisible by \(195318521017\), forcing its failure at \(249580077008\). Hence there must be a failure at some index \(n\geq3775\) (indeed, no later than \(249580077008\)). Since the OEIS conjecture asserts that all three displayed identities hold at every such index, the failure of this first identity disproves the conjecture.
